56	In BCS-controlled FewRel subsets, the high-BCS quartile shows $\Delta=-5.3$\,pp lower accuracy than low-BCS (quartile comparison; full data in Appendix~\ref{app:bcs-controlled-table}). At 80 relations, extreme-batch construction amplifies this to $-$31.2\,pp (CI: [17.7, 42.7]), stable across count levels. An intermediate count${}\,=\,40$ evaluation (40-relation subsets sampled from the 80-relation pool) yields consistent gaps ($-$33.3\,pp at count 8, $-$31.8\,pp at count 16), confirming monotonic decline.
57	
58	\paragraph{Document-level RE (DocRED).}
59	The effect replicates on DocRED's 96-relation schema: BCS gap $-$23.3\,pp at count 16 (slope $= -0.713$, $\rho = -0.661$, $p < 0.001$) and $-$17.6\,pp at count 32 (slope $= -0.690$, $\rho = -0.509$, $p = 0.002$). BCS explains 44--53\% of cross-batch variance ($R^2 = 0.525$ at count 16), substantially higher than FewRel ($R^2 = 0.218$), possibly reflecting a wider confusability range in the DocRED schema, though document-level context may also provide richer cues for type confusion. Across all RE settings, BCS slopes range from $-$0.40 to $-$0.71, significant in all conditions with sufficient BCS range.

15	(1)~Degradation operates along two dimensions: count-related recall decline (up to $-$49\,pp for document-level RE) and confusability-related type substitution (typical-batch gap ${\approx}\,2.2$\,pp), with count as the dominant factor. 4	Training-free\footnote{We use ``training-free'' and ``zero-shot'' interchangeably to denote prompting without parameter updates.}\footnote{Code and data will be released upon acceptance. Anonymous review materials: \url{https://anonymous.4open.science/r/schema-dag-extraction}} LLM information extraction (prompting a large language model with a target schema and asking it to extract structured information without any task-specific fine-tuning) enables rapid deployment across new domains and ontologies. This zero-shot paradigm eliminates the need for labeled data, and is attractive for applications where annotation is expensive or schemas evolve frequently \cite{llm4ie-survey-2024}. Yet the paradigm carries a critical limitation: performance degrades sharply as the number of candidate types in the prompt schema grows. On named entity recognition, recall drops from 0.72 with a single candidate type to a plateau of ${\sim}$0.27 across intermediate schema sizes (22--44 types) before partial recovery at full-schema. On relation extraction, accuracy falls from 85.7\% with one relation to 49.5\% with 80 relations (sentence-level) and from 88.0\% to 38.7\% with 96 relations (document-level), near or exceeding halving. This degradation is not academic: real-world ontologies routinely define 50--200+ types, which places them squarely in the regime where training-free extraction becomes unreliable.
5	
6	What explains this degradation? Our experiments yield four findings:
(1)~Degradation operates along two dimensions: count-related recall decline (up to $-$49\,pp for document-level RE) and confusability-related type substitution (typical-batch gap ${\approx}\,2.2$\,pp), with count as the dominant factor. The two dimensions exhibit bounded association in RE (Two One-Sided Tests [TOST] equivalence, $p = 0.003$ at $\pm 3$\,pp) but are coupled in NER.
(2)~Pairwise SCS predicts type confusion across NER, RE, and ED ($r = 0.112$--$0.129$); at batch level, BCS predicts accuracy in RE ($R^2 = 0.22$--$0.53$) but not in NER (batch-level $r \approx 0$, n.s.); per-type aggregation is confounded by centrality on homogeneous schemas (\S\ref{sec:centrality_confound}).
(3)~Effects are consistent across schema sizes and granularities (BCS slopes: $p = 0.60$; DocRED: $R^2 = 0.53$) and directionally consistent across prompt designs.
(4)~Schema decomposition fails due to merge amplification in NER; RE confusability-aware grouping yields no significant improvement over random (+1.4\,pp, $p \approx 0.19$, n.s.) despite oracle routing that recovers +29.8\,pp.

6	
7	\paragraph{Why does embedding similarity predict LLM confusion?}
8	SCS captures semantic proximity in LLMs' type-resolution space. The unconditional pairwise $R^2$ is modest (1.3\% on Few-NERD, $r = 0.112$) because ${\sim}89\%$ of type pairs never produce mutual confusion; among the 11\% with nonzero confusion, conditional $R^2$ rises to 7\%. Correlated pair-level signals then aggregate at the batch level: a Monte Carlo simulation ($\rho_{\mathrm{SCS}} = 0.35$; Appendix~\ref{app:aggregation-sim}) predicts batch $R^2$ of 18--25\%, consistent with the observed 22--53\% in RE. SCS is thus a weak pair-level predictor but a practically useful batch-level screen. We hypothesize that the NER U-shape (\S\ref{sec:count_curves}) reflects a dual-task burden absent in RE: partial schemas require simultaneous span detection and type-membership filtering; at full-schema, filtering becomes vacuous and recall recovers. This confirms task-specific pathways.
9	
10	\paragraph{Task-dependent batch-level effects.}
11	While pairwise SCS predicts type confusion in both NER and RE, the batch-level BCS--performance relationship is RE-specific: BCS explains 22--53\% of cross-batch accuracy variance in RE but shows no significant correlation with NER F1 ($r \approx 0$, $n = 450$). We hypothesize this reflects the different error structures: RE errors are dominated by type substitution (IntraSub scales with BCS; \S\ref{sec:multi_channel}), so batch-level confusability directly predicts accuracy. NER errors are dominated by missed entities (43--65\% of errors), which correlate with count rather than confusability; pairwise SCS captures individual type confusion but this signal is diluted at the batch level by the overwhelming contribution of boundary detection failures. This task dependence has practical implications: BCS is a useful pre-hoc screening tool for RE schema design but not for NER, where count reduction is the primary lever. tool_args.old_string:
Schema-induced degradation in training-free LLM extraction operates along two dimensions: count-related recall decline (up to $-$49\,pp) and confusability-related type substitution (${\approx}\,2.2$\,pp in typical batches, up to $-$31\,pp under extreme construction). The two dimensions exhibit bounded association in RE (TOST $p = 0.003$ at $\pm 3$\,pp) but are coupled in NER, where type ambiguity and boundary detection interact. These patterns replicate across model scales (8B, 32B, 70B) and architecture families, including the proprietary Gemini 2.5 Flash for Dimension~1; Dimension~2 attenuates on smaller models but remains significant at 70B scale for RE.

The confusability effect is a structural property of the schema rather than a prompting deficit. Few-shot demonstrations do not reduce the gap; the BCS penalty widens under 5-shot prompting (+4.3\,pp, $p = 0.014$; Appendix~\ref{sec:appendix_fewshot_bcs}). Schema decomposition fails due to merge amplification in NER and routing failure in RE. BCS enables pre-hoc screening for RE schema design, but batch-level confusability does not predict NER performance; for NER, count reduction remains the primary lever.

These findings have two implications. First, practitioners deploying training-free extraction on schemas with $>$20 types should expect substantial accuracy loss; confusability-aware type pair screening can flag problematic RE schemas before deployment. Second, when confusability is inherent to the domain and cannot be resolved through schema restructuring, training-based approaches that learn type boundaries from data may be necessary.

Schema-induced degradation in training-free LLM extraction operates along two dimensions: count-related recall decline (up to $-$49\,pp) and confusability-related type substitution (${\approx}\,2.2$\,pp in typical batches, up to $-$31\,pp under extreme construction). The two dimensions exhibit bounded association in RE (TOST $p = 0.003$) but are coupled in NER. These patterns replicate across model scales (8B, 32B, 70B) and architecture families, including the proprietary Gemini 2.5 Flash; few-shot demonstrations do not reduce the confusability gap (+4.3\,pp under 5-shot, $p = 0.014$). Schema decomposition fails due to merge amplification (NER) and routing failure (RE); BCS enables pre-hoc screening for RE but not NER.

These findings have practical and methodological implications. Practitioners deploying training-free extraction on schemas with $>$20 types should expect substantial accuracy loss; confusability-aware screening can flag problematic RE schemas before deployment. When confusability is inherent to the domain and cannot be resolved through schema restructuring, training-based approaches that learn type boundaries from data may be necessary.

\paragraph{Boundary conditions.}
The decomposition applies to cross-domain schemas; same-domain schemas exhibit centrality confounding (\S\ref{sec:centrality_confound}). High-BCS accuracy converges to $\approx$51\% across models, which suggests a task-inherent difficulty ceiling; at count 80, the full-schema BCS is fixed, so confusability ceases to be a predictor. RE's separation may partly reflect its closed-set format; the effect generalizes to document-level RE (DocRED slope $-$0.71). Prompt design modulates but does not eliminate the effect (v2 gap: $-$25.5\,pp; Appendix~\ref{sec:appendix_prompt_sensitivity}). Cross-scale evidence (32B vs.\ 8B) shows Dimension~1 replicates fully while Dimension~2 attenuates on smaller models and drops to near-zero $R^2$ for NER on Llama-3.1-8B (Tables~\ref{tab:cross_model}--\ref{tab:cross_model_bcs}). Count-related degradation may partly reflect prompt length (per-type recall 0.586 vs.\ single-pass 0.368, consistent with lost-in-middle effects; \citealt{lost-in-middle-2024}; \citealt{levy-2024-same-task}).
tool_args.new_string:
\paragraph{Boundary conditions.}
The two-dimensional decomposition applies to cross-domain schemas; same-domain schemas exhibit centrality confounding (\S\ref{sec:centrality_confound}). High-BCS accuracy converges to $\approx$51\% across models (a task-inherent ceiling); at count 80, BCS is fixed and ceases to be a predictor. The effect generalizes to document-level RE (DocRED slope $-$0.71) and persists across prompt designs (v2 gap: $-$25.5\,pp; Appendix~\ref{sec:appendix_prompt_sensitivity}). Dimension~1 replicates across scales (8B--70B); Dimension~2 attenuates on smaller models (Tables~\ref{tab:cross_model}--\ref{tab:cross_model_bcs}).

tool_args.old_string: SCS captures semantic proximity in LLMs' type-resolution space. The unconditional pairwise $R^2$ is modest (1.3\% on Few-NERD, $r = 0.112$) because ${\sim}89\%$ of type pairs never produce mutual confusion; among the 11\% with nonzero confusion, conditional $R^2$ rises to 7\%. Correlated pair-level signals then aggregate at the batch level: a Monte Carlo simulation ($\rho_{\mathrm{SCS}} = 0.35$; Appendix~\ref{app:aggregation-sim}) predicts batch $R^2$ of 18--25\%, consistent with the observed 22--53\% in RE. SCS is thus a weak pair-level predictor but a practically useful batch-level screen. We hypothesize that the NER U-shape (\S\ref{sec:count_curves}) reflects a dual-task burden absent in RE: partial schemas require simultaneous span detection and type-membership filtering; at full-schema, filtering becomes vacuous and recall recovers. This confirms task-specific pathways.
